title: The quest to make steel strong against a tiny attacker

Steel underpins a lot of infrastructure in modern society, but it can be weakened by the element hydrogen. Credit: Puneet Vikram Singh, Nature and Concept Photographer/ Getty Images Modern society is completely reliant on steel. Its strength underpins our buildings, transportation systems, and efforts to tackle climate change. But steel has a surprising vulnerability to the smallest of atoms — hydrogen. Atoms of hydrogen penetrate steel and weaken its structure.Known as hydrogen embrittlement, this phenomenon poses dangers for many of steel’s applications, from springs in cars to the cables of suspension bridges. Perhaps most concerningly, it threatens efforts to switch to hydrogen fuel, a clean-burning alternative to fossil fuels, since it can weaken the pipelines and storage tanks for hydrogen gas.“Hydrogen embrittlement is not a new problem,” notes Kenichi Takai, a materials scientist at Sophia University in Tokyo, Japan. “But the transition to energy systems based on hydrogen makes it much more urgent to address the problem.”Atomic understandingHis research aims to understand precisely how the phenomenon occurs at the atomic level, and to develop strategies to prevent it.It’s an ambitious goal. Hydrogen embrittlement has been studied for decades, but debate continues about its underlying mechanisms. Probing the effect is difficult because the small size of hydrogen makes it hard to track its movements through steel. And after embrittled components break, the culprit often escapes from the material before it can be analysed in the lab.Takai’s team has developed a range of cutting-edge techniques to overcome these obstacles. That work is helping to reveal how embrittlement might be averted, which should lead to more resilient steel for the hydrogen economy of the future.Steel is an alloy composed of iron, carbon and other elements. By varying its composition, microscopic structure and the processes used to manufacture it, materials scientists can create many different types of steel for various applications. Some have very high strength, for example, while others are more ductile and can be drawn into wires.Steel contains microscopic crystalline grains of metal, and each grain consists of a lattice of atoms. Embrittlement occurs under mechanical loading when hydrogen atoms from hydrogen gas, water or other sources worm their way into the lattice or between the grains.Attack pointsThe hydrogen atoms move quickly through the metal and can become trapped at several kinds of lattice defects of which there are three important types — vacancies, dislocations and grain boundaries. A vacancy is a point where an iron atom is missing from the lattice; a dislocation is a line of distortion in the lattice; and a grain boundary is the interface between two grains.Takai has investigated how each type of defect influences hydrogen embrittlement.“Hydrogen embrittlement isn’t caused by one single mechanism,” he says. Instead, it is partly determined by the microstructure of the steel itself, so various forms of steel are attacked in different ways.“For each microstructure, the mechanism is different, and we can determine that,” he adds.A crack in steel induced by hydrogen embrittlement. Credit: Uwe Aranas/ Shutterstock Takai’s research has shown that hydrogen can stabilize vacancies, for example, so that they accumulate in the material and contribute to hydrogen embrittlement and loss of ductility1. Hydrogen can also change the motion and interaction of dislocations, affecting how the material distorts when stretched. And when hydrogen gathers at a grain boundary, it promotes fractures by weakening the binding between grains. “Even a very small amount of hydrogen can cause a surprisingly large reduction in fracture resistance, particularly in high-strength steels,” says Takai. “Some of the microstructural features that make steel very strong can also make it more sensitive to hydrogen.”High-strength steels generally contain a high density of microstructural features such as dislocations, interfaces and other lattice defects. Some of these features strengthen steel, but they can also interact strongly with hydrogen.Chilling discoveriesOne of the most important techniques in Takai’s lab is low-temperature thermal desorption spectrometry (L-TDS). His team developed the method to study where hydrogen is located in steel, how strongly it binds and how it moves around.Conventional thermal desorption spectroscopy involves heating a sample of steel that contains some hydrogen and measuring when that hydrogen is released. But these experiments usually start from room temperature and since hydrogen is so mobile, many of the atoms are lost before measurement begins, giving an incomplete picture of where it was located.L-TDS overcomes that problem by cooling steel samples to about −200 °C, freezing hydrogen atoms in place. The researchers then gradually warm the sample, monitoring when hydrogen is freed.Recent experiments have shown that hydrogen trapped at different lattice defects is released at different temperatures, allowing researchers to distinguish hydrogen associated with dislocations, grain boundaries and vacancies. “We can use hydrogen desorption behaviour as a kind of fingerprint of the defects,” says Takai.L-TDS also reveals how stress makes hydrogen move around inside steel. The researchers added traces of hydrogen to a sample of high-strength steel and then applied different levels of stress within the elastic region. They found that the stress-induced hydrogen redistribution increased the amount of hydrogen trapped on grain boundaries, promoting fracture between grains2.Their recent studies suggest that, in the plastic region, hydrogen is more likely to redistribute towards dislocations and vacancies, promoting fracture in grains rather between them3.Takai’s team is even using hydrogen as a tracer to study strain-induced defects in more detail. After straining a piece of metal, the team adds tiny amounts of hydrogen, which is preferentially trapped at defects that offer the highest binding energies. By controlling the amount of tracer hydrogen and analysing its desorption with L-TDS, the researchers can determine which kinds of defect sites the hydrogen occupied4.“Hydrogen becomes not only the cause of the problem, but also a tool for seeing the atomic-scale defects involved in the problem,” says Takai.From knowledge to predictionAll these insights should help to develop steels that resist hydrogen embrittlement. “The goal is not only to reduce the hydrogen content, but also to ensure that the hydrogen is in safer places5,” says Takai.One strategy for achieving this is to introduce microstructural features that trap hydrogen at relatively harmless sites, preventing it from reaching critical sites. “We also want to reduce vacancy formation, reduce harmful grain-boundary trapping, and minimize local stress concentrations,” says Takai.Traditionally, research into hydrogen embrittlement has often studied materials after they fracture. Takai now wants to focus on what happens before fractures begin — when the steel still looks perfectly normal, even though hydrogen is already redistributing and interacting with lattice defects inside the steel.By combining L-TDS, microscopy, mechanical testing and computational approaches, Takai hopes that his group can learn to anticipate and avert problems in steel components.“I’d like to move from understanding failure after it happens, to predicting dangerous conditions before failure occurs,” says Takai. “I think that’s essential for designing truly hydrogen-resistant materials.”
